bib.title: Use of LLMs for Illicit Purposes: Threats, Prevention Measures, and Vulnerabilities

read.skipped: Reference list (from char ~111678) skimmed for lineage only; the PDF has no appendix and no results tables.

question: What threats, prevention measures and vulnerabilities does the scientific literature describe for LLMs used for illicit purposes, and how do they relate?
contributions: A taxonomy relating threats (generative capabilities causing harm), prevention measures, and vulnerabilities arising from imperfect prevention (Fig 1).
An overview of predominantly scientific work in each category, with defined concepts and academic and real-world instances.
A discussion of public concern, theoretical limits of LLM safety, and future LLM-enabled security concerns.
A tally showing that many cited works are not peer-reviewed (Fig 2).

results.claim: Of 93 papers the survey cites across threats, preventions and vulnerabilities, 43 (about 46%) had not passed peer review.
results.setup: Papers cited in Sections 5-7 only; counted by the authors
results.quote: almost half of the discussed papers not being peer-reviewed (43 of 93, around 46%)

results.claim: Peer-review share falls from threats to preventions to vulnerabilities; only 3 of 15 vulnerability papers were peer-reviewed.
Hazell (2023) reports that generating 1,000 personalised phishing emails costs about $10 with Claude in about two hours; the survey notes there is no quantitative evaluation of the emails.
results.setup: Hazell (2023) demonstration on 600 UK MPs, conditioning GPT models on Wikipedia bios; qualitative examples only
results.quote: one can generate 1,000 phishing emails for $10 USD in around two hours

results.claim: Larger and more duplicated training data are memorised more; OPT 66B and GPT-Neo 6B complete almost 20% and 60% of training-set sequences respectively.
results.setup: Carlini et al. (2022): GPT-Neo, T5, OPT families; extraction prompts taken from training sets
results.quote: OPT 66B and GPT-Neo 6B correctly complete almost 20% and 60% of sequence inputs that were taken from the models’ training sets

results.claim: Differentially private fine-tuning cuts GPT-2 Large PII precision and recall from about 23%/30% to about 3% on law cases.
results.setup: Lukas et al. (2023): four GPT-2 sizes, three datasets, four million sampled tokens; PII extraction
results.quote: GPT-2 Large has a recall of 23% and a precision of 30% on the law cases dataset
results.note: After DP training the text says precision and recall are around 3%

results.claim: PII inference by GPT-2 Large is correct up to 70% without DP and 8% with DP.
results.setup: Lukas et al. (2023), PII inference with candidate list
results.quote: GPT-2 Large can correctly predict up to 70% of PII without DP, and 8% with DP training

results.claim: Red-team data: 324 crowdworkers produced 38,961 attacks on models of 2.7B, 23B and 52B parameters; no model type was robust.
results.setup: Ganguli et al. (2022); plain LM, HHH-prompted, rejection sampling (best of 16), RLHF; recruited from MTurk and Upwork

results.claim: LLM-driven red teaming: zero-shot prompting yields 3.7% offensive replies while reinforcement learning yields around 40%.
results.setup: Perez et al. (2022): Gopher 280B target, another Gopher as red LLM, 500,000 generated completions, harm classifier
results.quote: zero-shot prompting generating a fraction of 3.7% offensive texts

results.claim: LLaMA-2 fully refuses almost 40% of the safe prompts in XSTest versus 6% for GPT-4 (exaggerated safety).
results.metric: full refusal rate on safe prompts
results.setup: Rottger et al. (2023): 200 safe prompts, 20 in each of 10 categories
results.quote: fully refusing almost 40% of the safe prompts in XSTEST

results.claim: OpenAI's AI-text detector scored AUC 0.97 in distribution but 0.66 on an out-of-distribution challenge set.
results.setup: OpenAI (2023a) classifier trained on 34 language models
results.quote: yielded an AUC score of 0.97, while on an out-of-distribution (OOD) challenge set, the score dropped to 0.66

results.claim: Prompt leaking succeeds above 60% across GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Vicuna-13B using five manual prompts; a 5-gram overlap filter defends but can be evaded by ciphers.
results.setup: Zhang and Ippolito (2023): paired secret-prompt and user-query datasets
results.quote: success rates of above 60% across all models and datasets

results.claim: Self-correction through instruction appears at about 22B parameters.
results.setup: Ganguli et al. (2023): RLHF models 810M to 175B on BBQ, Winogender and a new discrimination dataset
results.quote: self-correction behavior appears at a model size of around 22B parameters

results.claim: Shen et al. found 666 jailbreak prompts in six months from four online sources; moderation endpoints, OpenChatKit and NeMo-Guardrails only marginally reduce success.
results.setup: Shen et al. (2023a): Reddit, Discord, FlowGPT and others; 46,000 GPT-4-generated test questions

results.claim: Wei et al. attribute jailbreaks to two failure modes, competing objectives and mismatched generalisation, and argue scaling alone will not make models safer.
results.setup: Wei et al. (2023): GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Claude v1.3; 32 red-team prompts and 317 held-out GPT-4 prompts

results.claim: Universal GCG suffixes optimised on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat and Vicuna-7B transfer to Pythia, Falcon, Guanaco, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and PaLM-2.
results.setup: Zou et al. (2023): harmful strings and harmful behaviours datasets

results.claim: A theoretical result: any mechanism that does not fully eliminate unwanted behaviour leaves the model open to adversarial prompt attacks.
results.quote: any mechanism to address unwanted behaviors of LLMs that does not fully eliminate them leaves the model susceptible to adversarial prompt attacks

results.claim: Taxonomy: threats arise from generative capabilities, preventions control them, vulnerabilities arise from imperfect preventions and re-enable threats.
results.setup: Figure 1 taxonomy, scope limited to intended attacks and mostly scientific literature
results.quote: Such vulnerabilities then re-enable existing threats.

results.claim: VPI poisoning of 1% of Alpaca 7B instruction data steers sentiment, injects code and elicits chain-of-thought.
results.setup: Yan et al. (2023) against Alpaca 7B; defenses: Alpagasus data filtering (more effective) and an inference-time anti-bias instruction (slightly effective)
results.quote: when 1% of the training data are poisoned

limits: Authors cannot guarantee completeness: papers were found from the authors' knowledge and expertise, not a systematic search (Sec 4).
Mixes peer-reviewed papers with preprints and news articles; 43 of 93 cited works were not peer-reviewed, 12 of 15 in the vulnerabilities section.
Considers only intended attacks where adversaries deliberately exploit LLMs; excludes unintended bugs and inherent errors (Sec 2).
No new experiments; all numbers are quoted from other studies, several on 2022-2023 models (GPT-2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude v1.3, LLaMA-2) and dated by later defences and attacks.
Defences against data poisoning are mostly evaluated on BERT-sized models, not billion-parameter LLMs (Sec 6.7).
Scope is text; images, robotics and financial markets are out of scope; diffusion-model memorisation is only mentioned.
Hazell (2023) phishing claims rest on qualitative examples only.
practices: Treat system prompts as retrievable: assume prompt leaking and goal hijacking are possible, and add an output overlap check (5-gram overlap with the system prompt) while knowing ciphers evade it (Sec 7.1).
Deduplicate training data and consider differentially private fine-tuning to reduce memorisation and PII leakage (Sec 5.5, 6.6).
Filter instruction-tuning data for quality (Alpagasus) to reduce poisoning success such as VPI (Sec 5.6).
Hash crawled sources of URL-indexed web datasets and compare against the intended source to counter dataset poisoning (Carlini et al. 2023b, Sec 7.1).
Red team with humans and with LLMs, since no model type was robust in either (Sec 6.2).
Weigh the helpfulness-harmlessness trade-off and exaggerated refusal when tuning for safety (Sec 6.4, 8.2).
Do not rely on AI-text detectors alone: paraphrasing evades them and they misclassify non-native English writing (Sec 6.1).
Treat content filters and moderation endpoints as insufficient against jailbreaks (Sec 7.2).
Prefer peer-reviewed evidence when prioritising concerns (Sec 8.1, 9).

terms.definition: Generative capabilities of LLMs causing harm (e.g., generating phishing emails, malware, misinformation).
Measures to prevent threats (e.g., RLHF, red teaming).
Unintended LLM behavior that is exploited for malicious use; defined as flaws resulting from imperfect prevention measures.
The practice of extracting or manipulating an LLM's system prompt directly via prompting; split into prompt leaking (extraction) and goal hijacking (manipulation).
The practice of engineering prompts that yield undesirable LLM behavior; does not require access to the system prompt.
The deliberate introduction of malicious examples into a training dataset with the intention to manipulate the learning outcome of the model.
Training on poisoned examples so that the model predicts a particular class whenever a specific trigger phrase is present.
Collective efforts that deliberately attempt to identify safety-related issues of LLM-based systems, by humans or by LLMs.
Wei et al.'s two jailbreak failure modes: safety conflicts with pre-training and instruction-following objectives; or inputs are out-of-distribution for safety training but not pre-training.
NCSC vulnerability types: unintended functionality from poor design, intended functionality attackers misuse, and mistakes by system users.
